questions.question: What symbol represents universal quantifier?
questions.explanation: ∀ means for all.

questions.question: What symbol represents existential quantifier?
questions.explanation: ∃ means there exists.

questions.question: What does ∀x P(x) mean?
options: There exists x such that P(x)
For all x, P(x) is true
For some x, P(x) is true
questions.explanation: Universal quantifier applies to all elements.

questions.question: What does ∃x P(x) mean?
options: For all x, P(x) is true
At least one x satisfies P(x)
questions.explanation: Existential quantifier requires at least one.

questions.question: What is the domain of discourse?
options: The set of all possible values for variables
questions.explanation: Domain is the universe of values.

questions.question: What is the negation of ∀x P(x)?
questions.explanation: Not all becomes there exists not.

questions.question: What is the negation of ∃x P(x)?
questions.explanation: There exists not becomes for all not.

questions.question: What is the scope of a quantifier?
options: The part of formula it applies to
questions.explanation: Scope is the reach of quantifier.

questions.question: What is a bound variable?
questions.explanation: Bound variables are quantified.

questions.question: What is a free variable?
questions.explanation: Free variables are not quantified.

questions.question: What does ∀x∃y L(x,y) mean?
options: There is one x related to every y
For every x there is a y such that L(x,y)
questions.explanation: ∀ then ∃: each x gets some possibly different y.

questions.question: What does ∃x∀y L(x,y) mean?
options: For every x there is a y
Every y relates to some x
There is an x such that L(x,y) holds for all y
No x relates to all y
questions.explanation: A single x works for every y.

questions.question: What is the negation of ∀x∃y P(x,y)?
questions.explanation: Push negation inward, flipping each quantifier.

questions.question: On an empty domain, what is the truth value of ∀x P(x)?
questions.explanation: Universal claims hold vacuously on empty domains.

questions.question: On an empty domain, what is the truth value of ∃x P(x)?
questions.explanation: No element exists to witness P.

questions.question: What does ∃!x P(x) assert?
options: At least one x satisfies P
At most one x satisfies P
questions.explanation: ∃! means unique existence.

questions.question: If 'All students passed' is false, what must be true?
questions.explanation: The negation is ∃x ¬P(x).

questions.question: In ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)), what is the scope of ∀x?
questions.explanation: Parentheses delimit the quantifier's scope.

questions.question: What is needed to disprove ∀x P(x)?
options: A proof that ¬P holds for all x
questions.explanation: One counterexample refutes a universal claim.

questions.question: What establishes ∃x P(x)?
questions.explanation: One witness proves existence.

questions.question: Translate 'Every student knows programming' where S(x) = 'x is a student' and P(x) = 'x knows programming'.
questions.explanation: Universal statements pair with implication.

questions.question: Translate 'Some student knows programming'.
questions.explanation: Existential statements pair with conjunction.

questions.question: Why is ∃x(S(x)→P(x)) a poor translation of 'Some student knows programming'?
options: It is true whenever a non-student exists
It requires all students to program
questions.explanation: A non-student makes the implication vacuously true.

questions.question: What does ∀x∀y P(x,y) require?
options: P holds for at least one pair
P holds for every ordered pair
P holds only when x = y
questions.explanation: Both variables range over the whole domain.

questions.question: Which formula is equivalent to ¬∀x¬P(x)?
questions.explanation: Quantifier duality: ¬∀x¬P(x) ≡ ∃x P(x).

questions.question: What does ∀x∈S P(x) express?
options: P holds for all elements of S
P holds for elements outside S
questions.explanation: Restricted quantification limits the range to S.

questions.question: Translate 'No hacker who is caught goes unpunished' using H(x) = hacker, C(x) = caught, P(x) = punished.
questions.explanation: 'No X is unpunished' means every caught hacker is punished: universally quantify with a conjunction in the antecedent.

questions.question: On the domain {1,2}, evaluate ∀x∃y(x·y = 2).
options: False — no single y works for all x
True — each x finds a witness in the domain
True — because y = 2 is a fixed witness
questions.explanation: For x=1 take y=2; for x=2 take y=1. Each x may choose a different y, so the sentence holds.

questions.question: What is the correct negation of ∀x∃y(x<y), with negation pushed inward?
questions.explanation: ¬∀x∃y(x<y) = ∃x∀y¬(x<y) = ∃x∀y(x≥y): some x has no y above it.

questions.question: A proof has ∀x(P(x)→Q(x)) and obtains ∃xP(x) with witness d. Can it conclude Q(d)?
options: No — the universal must be instantiated at a different constant
Yes — instantiate the universal at d, then apply modus ponens to P(d)
No — existential witnesses cannot be named
Only if d is provably equal to every x
questions.explanation: Universal instantiation works for any domain element, including the witness d; P(d) plus P(d)→Q(d) gives Q(d).

questions.question: Compare 'every student passed some exam' (∀s∃e P(s,e)) with 'some exam was passed by every student' (∃e∀s P(s,e)). How do they relate?
options: The first is stronger and implies the second
The second is stronger and implies the first
questions.explanation: One exam serving all students guarantees each student passed something; the reverse needs a common witness, which may not exist.
